findings.title: Findings converge on the harness-vs-generated recap arbiter and the `current` flag
findings.why_it_matters: Three findings from both critics land on one mechanism: D2's "one function picks the harness recap when current, the generated one otherwise", which feeds the generator's harness exemption (D4) and the public `source`/`current` fields (D6). Finding 3 says delete the harness source. Finding 4 says the pick is undefined when neither recap is current. Finding 5 says `current` is inferred from a database that lags the transcript, and then published. Is the arbiter itself the problem? It decides between two sources about which one is current, which is the shape the 010 retrospective blames. Should it be re-evaluated as a whole (whether it's needed, what it promises consumers, which failure modes are worth handling and which to accept and document) instead of patched three times?
findings.recommended: B: Keep the arbiter and address Findings 3, 4, 5 individually.
findings.chosen: B: Keep the arbiter and address Findings 3, 4, 5 individually.

findings.title: Findings converge on imported rows as a proxy for a session's live state
findings.why_it_matters: Both critics flag the same habit (structural-minimalist F4: "state is inferred from partial evidence in two places"; senior-engineer F3: "this is inferred state"). Whether a session is idle (D3) and whether a recap is current (D2/D6) are both read from the last imported message, but sync runs only on Stop and import only at SessionStart, so the database trails the transcript. The trailing is worst in the restore case: a session killed mid-turn has its last turn unimported until the next SessionStart import, and the boot run (`--idle-minutes 0`) runs before that. Does treating imported rows as the session's live state need re-evaluating, or is the lag a limitation to accept and document?
findings.recommended: B: Keep imported rows as the proxy and address Findings 5 and 12 individually.
findings.chosen: Other: add D9, backfill recaps imports before selecting

findings.title: Drop the `away_summary` source, its columns, and the `source`/`current` fields
findings.why_it_matters: D2 adds two `branches` columns, a parse-boundary change (suffix stripping, latest-on-chain), a shared pick-the-recap function, D4's harness exemption, and two public read fields (`source`, `current`). All of it exists to skip calls for the third of sessions with a current harness recap. Without it, the read returns `session_id, text, as_of` and the contract that D6 calls hard to reverse gets smaller. The design itself says the consumer gets its ids from Claude Code's session files (design.md:134), so it already holds the transcripts where the harness recap lives. The case against dropping it: the evaluation used the harness recap as the reference, and generated recaps matched its next step only 15/20 and 10-11/15 times (evaluation.md:15, :23-25). So for that third of sessions, dropping the harness source means a worse recap plus a call.
findings.recommended: A: Keep D2 as ratified and pin its pick rule (Finding 4 A).
findings.chosen: A: Keep D2 as ratified and pin its pick rule (Finding 4 A).

findings.title: Precedence between a stale harness recap and a generated recap is undefined
findings.why_it_matters: D2 says the read returns the harness recap "when it's current and the generated one otherwise". It doesn't say what happens when neither is current: a harness recap older than a generated one, a stale harness recap with no generated one, or a harness recap newer than a stale generated one. The read could show a recap two turns behind while a newer one exists. D2 promises that the read and the generator's exemption (D4) use the same function, but that function's rule is one clause. Leaving it unspecified is the 010 retrospective's failure shape (an unmodeled state machine).
findings.recommended: A: Specify in D2: of the session's harness and generated recaps, the one with the newest `as_of` wins; the read returns it, and the generator skips a session only when that winner covers the branch's last imported message.
findings.chosen: A: Specify in D2: of the session's harness and generated recaps, the one with the newest `as_of` wins; the read returns it, and the generator skips a session only when that winner covers the branch's last imported message.

findings.title: `current` is inferred from imported rows that lag the transcript, and published as a public field
findings.why_it_matters: A harness recap counts as current "when nothing on the chain comes after it" (design.md:87), and a generated one when it covers the branch's last message, but both are measured against imported rows. Claude Code writes `away_summary` three minutes after a turn ends, which is after that turn's Stop sync. A user who comes back, starts a turn, and is killed mid-turn leaves a database where the harness recap still looks last. The session is exempted from generation (design.md:107) and `show-recaps` reports `current: true` for a recap that is behind, which is the restore case D3 says matters most. A generated recap has the same lag against an unsynced tail, so dropping the harness source alone doesn't fix it. `current` becomes a public JSON field consumers will trust, and D6 calls that contract hard to reverse.
findings.recommended: A: Drop `current` from D6's output; keep `as_of` as the time of the last message the recap covers, and keep the currency test internal to selection.

findings.title: D5 counts run-level failures as per-session failures, so a lapsed login or rate limit cools down the week's sessions for a day
findings.why_it_matters: D5 gives every failed session a 24-hour cooldown and aborts after 3 consecutive failures. The ratified acceptance ("the sessions hit before an abort also wait a day") prices one abort. But the timer fires every ~20 minutes and each run reaches the next 3 uncooled sessions. A login that lapses overnight cools 3 sessions per run, 9 an hour, about 70 over 8 hours, which is most of a week's eligible sessions. After logging back in, almost nothing generates for up to a day, and there is no way to clear the cooldowns (purge is out of scope). That defeats the stated intent that systemd owns run-level retries: the next tick retries different sessions while the earlier ones wait a day. The reverse case also bites: three sessions that fail on their own (oversize input, Finding 8) at the head of the queue end a healthy run `failed`, and `doctor` reports `recaps-failed` for something the user can't fix.
findings.recommended: A: Split D5's failures into run-level (not logged in, rate limited, `claude` missing) and per-session. A run-level error ends the run `failed` and writes no cooldown. A per-session error records the 24 h cooldown and the run continues. The 3-consecutive abort stays as a backstop for anything misclassified.
findings.chosen: A: Split D5's failures into run-level (not logged in, rate limited, `claude` missing) and per-session. A run-level error ends the run `failed` and writes no cooldown. A per-session error records the 24 h cooldown and the run continues. The 3-consecutive abort stays as a backstop for anything misclassified.

findings.title: `exclude_projects` doesn't cover sessions imported before exclusion, and the project's data-sensitivity statement says transcripts are never transmitted
findings.why_it_matters: The Posture says "content only goes to Claude for sessions ccrecall has imported, so `exclude_projects` keeps applying." Exclusion is only enforced at write time: `import_project` returns early for an excluded project and `sync_current` skips an excluded cwd, and neither removes stored rows. The README says so too: "Conversations stored before you excluded a project stay stored." The generator reads imported rows, so a project the user excluded after it was imported still gets selected (if active within `--days`), and its content goes to Anthropic, silently. Also, this feature is the first to send transcript content off the machine. CLAUDE.md's frontmatter says transcripts stay "on the user's machine, never transmitted", and the README's privacy wording covers only the local embedding path. Both statements become false when recaps ship.
findings.recommended: A: Add to D4: selection skips sessions whose project matches the current `exclude_projects`, by the same rule import uses. Correct the Posture's Hardening line, and add the README and CLAUDE.md `data-sensitivity` updates to the Docs build step.
findings.chosen: A: Add to D4: selection skips sessions whose project matches the current `exclude_projects`, by the same rule import uses. Correct the Posture's Hardening line, and add the README and CLAUDE.md `data-sensitivity` updates to the Docs build step.

findings.title: Generation input has no size bound
findings.why_it_matters: A branch with null compaction columns (synced before this change and never since) sends the whole branch, including `tool_content`. The output is capped at 400 characters but the input isn't capped at all. The risk concentrates in compacted sessions with null columns: their whole branch is the full pre-compaction history, which by definition outgrew the live context window. Such an input fails the same way every time, costs a cooldown (and under D5 as ratified counts toward an abort, Finding 6), and bills the whole input against the subscription. An uncompacted session fit in the live context, so it's less exposed.
findings.recommended: A: Add to Assumed: the input is capped at a fixed size; it leads with `compact_summary` when present, otherwise the first user turn, then the most recent rows that fit.
findings.chosen: Other: prose-only input (no notifications or tool_content, no per-message caps) with a 400,000-character head+tail cap
findings.choice_reason: Chose after measuring input composition and probing four shapes on one session plus five notification-heavy sessions

findings.title: Drop D1's compaction columns in favor of a head-plus-tail input
findings.why_it_matters: D1 adds `compact_summary` and `compact_boundary_at`, a `SCHEMA_VERSION` 9 to 10 delta, a parse-boundary change, and two input paths (post-compaction versus whole branch). The quality evidence is thin: in run 2 (n=15) post-compaction beats full input by one session on next-step (11 vs 10 same, 1 vs 2 different), with goal and recognizability tied, and run 1's two compacted misses improved (one fixed, one partly). The structural-minimalist proposes building the input from the first user turn plus the last rows, with no schema or parser change. Two of its supporting claims are weaker than stated. First, the evaluation says latency is not a constraint (evaluation.md:35), not cost. The 0.65x cost cuts usage on a subscription whose limits Finding 6 shows are routine. Second, the parse change adds fields to the branch dict without changing `active_chain`'s entries, so no `ACTIVE_CHAIN_VERSION` bump (design.md:191). The senior-engineer's pushback calls D1 ratified and additive.
findings.recommended: B: Replace D1 with a head-plus-tail input built from existing rows, after one probe run comparing it with the post-compaction input.
findings.chosen: B: Replace D1 with a head-plus-tail input built from existing rows, after one probe run comparing it with the post-compaction input.
findings.choice_reason: Chose after a head-to-head on 8 compacted sessions (evaluation.md run 4) showed equal quality

findings.title: A recap row's behavior on a failed regeneration, and when it records what it covers, are unspecified
findings.why_it_matters: D5 puts `error` and `attempted_at` on the session's `recaps` row, and D3 puts the last-message time the recap covers on that same row. The design never says whether a failed regeneration replaces a good recap's text, which would lose the session's last good recap. It also doesn't say when the covered-through time is captured. If it's read at write time, after a several-second call during which sync committed new rows, the recap claims to cover messages it never saw, and D3's "changed since" predicate never selects it again until the next change.
findings.chosen: Add one bullet to `## Assumed`: "A recap's covered-through time is read in the same read as its input and written with its text. A failed regeneration records `error` and `attempted_at` and never clears or replaces an existing `text`; a success clears `error`." Evidence pointer: D3's stored column and D5's stored columns.

findings.title: Does `backfill recaps` need its own run-history kind?
findings.why_it_matters: D8 adds a run kind, a job key, and a `doctor` finding for an opt-in command, while `backfill summaries` and `backfill tool-content` have none. The cheaper alternative: `doctor` reads the most recent `recaps.error`. On the other side, the job lock is required by CLAUDE.md's one-job-lock rule anyway, run history is the only place an expired login surfaces unattended, and the embedding backfill already provides the pattern. The critic leans keep.

findings.title: "Idle" is inferred from the last imported message
findings.why_it_matters: D3 treats a session as idle when its last imported message is 30+ minutes old. A turn that runs 30+ minutes without ending (a long tool call or subagent run) syncs nothing until its Stop, so it looks idle and gets a recap mid-turn. That recap is replaced after the next idle break, so the cost is one extra call and a briefly mid-turn recap.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a turn quiet for longer than `--idle-minutes` gets a recap mid-turn, replaced after the next idle break at the cost of one call.

findings.title: `--no-session-persistence` is the only guard against recap calls being imported, and it fails open
findings.why_it_matters: If a Claude Code or SDK release stops honoring `--no-session-persistence` passed through `extra_args`, every recap call leaves a transcript holding its whole input, and ccrecall imports it. These one-turn sessions fall below D4's 3-turn floor, so they won't be recapped, but they duplicate other sessions' content into search and the index. The probe produced 146 of them, and they had to be purged by hand. No purge command exists (out of scope), so recovering means editing the database by hand. The design's test pins the argument passed, not the CLI's behavior.
findings.recommended: A: Run every generation call with a dedicated working directory under `~/.ccrecall/`, and have import always skip that directory's project.
findings.chosen: A: Run every generation call with a dedicated working directory under `~/.ccrecall/`, and have import always skip that directory's project.

findings.title: Refusals and apologies would be stored as recaps
findings.why_it_matters: D5's situation already treats empty or malformed output as a failure, but nothing catches a short refusal ("I can't help with that"), which would be stored as the recap, shown by the picker, and not retried until the session changes. The 400-character truncation can also cut mid-word. In the probe, all 35 generated recaps were under 400 characters and none was a refusal (evaluation.md:15, :35).
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a refusal or apology from the model is stored as the recap until the session changes.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a refusal or apology from the model is stored as the recap until the session changes.

findings.title: D7's base dependency puts ~330 MB and ~0.6 s on every install for an opt-in feature
findings.why_it_matters: **Audience assumption:** public library with real installs; accepted +330 MB and +0.6 s on every CLI invocation is a tradeoff for an open-source package with many users who will never run recaps. The ratified C is the only D7 option that charges every user, including the detached `sync-current` on every Stop, for a feature that "does nothing until the user runs the command." The senior-engineer adds that it also puts a bundled binary (supply-chain surface) in every install, and that each recap call starts a headless Claude Code process that can run alongside the embedding backfill. That process's memory wasn't measured and is far below the backfill's ~8 GB peak. The user chose C after seeing these costs in D7's table.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: every install carries the SDK (~330 MB) and every `ccrecall` CLI invocation pays ~0.6 s, whether or not recaps are used.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: every install carries the SDK (~330 MB) and every `ccrecall` CLI invocation pays ~0.6 s, whether or not recaps are used.
